Understanding lactose intolerance

Author: Healthy Food Guide
Save to favs
Log in now in to enjoy this feature
See favs

In summary

  • Lactose intolerance differs from a milk allergy, causing digestive discomfort like bloating and gas rather than an immune reaction.
  • Managing symptoms often involves food swaps, such as lactose-free dairy, fortified plant milks or naturally low-lactose foods like aged cheeses and live-culture yoghurt.
  • Cutting dairy makes it essential to source enough calcium elsewhere, whether through fortified alternatives, tofu, canned fish with bones or leafy greens.

Lactose intolerance affects many people, making it difficult to digest milk and dairy products. While the condition can cause discomfort, the good news is that it’s manageable with a few dietary adjustments. This article explores what lactose intolerance is, how it differs from a milk allergy and how to maintain a balanced diet by incorporating lactose-free alternatives and ensuring you’re getting enough calcium.

Lactose intolerance vs milk allergy

It’s important to differentiate between lactose intolerance and a milk allergy, as the two are often confused but are very different conditions.

Milk allergy

A dairy allergy is an immune system reaction to the proteins in milk, such as casein or whey. It can cause severe symptoms such as hives, swelling, vomiting and, in extreme cases, anaphylaxis. This is a potentially life-threatening condition, especially for infants and young children. While most children will outgrow their milk allergy by the time they reach three years of age, it remains a common food allergy in babies.

Lactose intolerance

Lactose intolerance is different: It occurs when your body cannot fully digest lactose, the sugar naturally found in milk and many dairy products. This usually happens because your body doesn’t produce enough lactase, the enzyme responsible for breaking down lactose in the small intestine. When lactose isn’t digested properly, it passes into the large intestine, where it’s fermented by bacteria, often leading to uncomfortable symptoms.

Symptoms include:

  • Bloating
  • Gas
  • Abdominal pain
  • Diarrhoea
  • Nausea
  • Rumbling stomach sounds

Lactose intolerance is generally less serious than a milk allergy, but it can still cause a lot of discomfort. Importantly, people with lactose intolerance can usually tolerate small amounts of lactose without significant issues.

Think you might be lactose intolerant?

Start with a symptom diary: Keep track of what you eat and drink, particularly higher-lactose foods, and any symptoms you notice afterwards, such as bloating, abdominal pain or diarrhoea.

Check your symptoms: If you regularly notice symptoms after consuming high-lactose foods, such as a milkshake or glass of milk, you may have lactose intolerance. Everyone has a different level of lactose tolerance, so the amount that triggers symptoms can vary.

If symptoms persist, speak with a GP to determine if lactose intolerance is the cause. It is also worthwhile working with a dietitian to identify your individual lactose tolerance and find suitable alternatives to ensure you’re still getting enough calcium and vitamin D.

How lactose intolerance is treated

Lactose intolerance can be managed by making adjustments to your diet, including reducing dairy or avoiding some foods.  This may involve a bit of trial and error to see what works for you, as some people find they can tolerate some milk or milk products.  An accredited practising or registered dietitian can help support this process.  For instance, you may find you can tolerate yoghurt with live cultures, some cheese that is naturally lower in lactose or combining small amounts of dairy with a main meal. Completely avoiding lactose foods can actually make symptoms of intolerance worse if you accidentally consume dairy.  Figuring out how to include a little lactose in your diet can help you grow good gut bacteria that help break down lactose, decreasing your chances of symptoms through accidental or intentional lactose exposure.  If you have been completely dairy free, it’s best to very slowly but regularly reintroduce small amounts of lactose-containing foods to make sure your gut bacteria have time to adjust.

Lactase tablets or drops

Some people find taking lactase tablets or drop can help if there’s an occasion where you need to eat dairy.  These are not recommended for daily use though and may not be suitable for young children and pregnant or breastfeeding people.

What is lactose anyway?

Lactose is a naturally occurring sugar found in milk and dairy products. It is classified as a disaccharide, which means it’s composed of two simpler sugars: glucose and galactose. To digest lactose, your body needs the enzyme lactase, which breaks it down into these simpler sugars. If lactase levels are low or absent, the lactose cannot be digested properly, causing digestive discomfort.

It’s important to note that if you like dairy foods, you don’t have to cut them out altogether. Understanding what foods are high in lactose and familiarising yourself with the many lactose-free alternatives available means you can still enjoy these foods without the offending sugar.

Common foods that contain lactose

Dairy products are the most common sources of lactose. The amount of lactose in different dairy products varies and some are easier to tolerate than others:

  • Milk (cow, goat, sheep)
  • Ice cream
  • Yoghurt
  • Cream
  • Soft cheeses like cream cheese, ricotta, and cottage cheese.

Cheeses that have been aged for longer, such as cheddar, parmesan and Swiss, tend to have very low or virtually no lactose because the lactose is broken down during the fermentation process. Yoghurt made with live cultures can also be lower in lactose because live bacteria can break it down.

Hidden lactose in processed foods

Lactose can also appear in unexpected places, especially in processed foods. Many packaged products use dairy ingredients such as whey or milk solids as fillers, stabilisers or flavour enhancers. Be on the lookout for these ingredients in:

  • Baked goods
  • Processed meats like sausages
  • Some breakfast cereals and muesli bars
  • Certain medications and supplements.

When managing lactose intolerance, always check food labels for dairy-derived ingredients, even if the product isn’t a typical dairy item.

Food swaps to help manage symptoms

Reduce or limit lactose

The first step in managing lactose intolerance is to reduce or limit dairy in your diet. While many people with lactose intolerance can tolerate small amounts of lactose, larger quantities are likely to trigger symptoms. You may find that you can comfortably drink a small glass of milk (100-200ml) with a meal or snack on yoghurt with live cultures.

Lactose-free dairy products are also great option for those with lactose intolerance. These products have the lactase enzyme added, which breaks down the lactose before you consume them.

Lactose-free milks

Lactose-free dairy milks are available, so you can still enjoy the benefits of milk such as calcium, protein and other important nutrients. Additionally, there are now a good variety of plant-based milk alternatives. Always look for versions that are fortified with calcium. We recommend choosing a fortified milk alternative that contains 120mg or more calcium per 100ml. Some popular milk substitutes include:

  • Soy milk: A nutrient-dense option that’s closest to dairy milk in protein and carbs. For soy-based milk alternatives, we recommend choosing those containing 3g or more protein per 100ml.
  • Almond milk: Light and low in calories, often fortified with calcium and vitamin D.
  • Oat milk: Slightly creamier than most other plant milks and works well in cooking, since it doesn’t break down with heat. Low in protein, with a medium GI (69).
  • Rice milk: Easily digestible but contains only a trace of protein. It has a high glycaemic index (GI) of 79–92 and is higher in carbs than other plant milks.

Non-dairy cheeses

These can be made from nuts or soy and are available in various textures and flavours, making them suitable for different uses like spreading or melting. However, as mentioned, some cheeses, such as mozzarella, cheddar, Swiss, parmesan, brie and blue, are naturally lower in lactose, so you may want to experiment with them first.

Other lactose-free foods

Most whole foods are naturally lactose-free. These include:

  • Lean meat, fish, eggs and poultry
  • Fruits and vegetables
  • Grains like rice, oats, and quinoa
  • Nuts and seeds.

These foods can form the foundation of a balanced, lactose-free diet.

Getting enough calcium

If you eliminate or reduce dairy in your diet, ensuring you still get enough calcium is essential. Calcium plays a crucial role in healthy bones, muscle function and maintaining heart health.

Daily calcium requirements

The recommended dietary intake (RDI) for calcium varies by age and gender:

  • Adults: 1000 mg per day
  • Teens and older adults: 1300 mg per day
  • Pregnant and breastfeeding women: 1000-1300 mg per day

Calcium-rich non-dairy foods

Fortunately, there are dairy-free foods that are naturally rich in calcium or fortified with it, that can help you meet your calcium needs:

  • Fortified plant milks: Soy, almond, and oat milks are often fortified with calcium and vitamin D.
  • Tofu: A great plant protein source, especially when made with calcium sulphate.
  • Canned fish with bones: Sardines and salmon are excellent sources of calcium.
  • Leafy green vegetables: Kale, collard greens, and broccoli are good plant-based sources of calcium, though not all greens have the same bioavailability.
  • Almonds, sesame seeds, and tahini: These are rich in calcium and can be easily added to meals and snacks.

If you’re struggling to meet your calcium needs through food alone, you may need to discuss calcium supplementation with your doctor or dietitian. But it’s best to aim for calcium-rich foods first, as they provide additional nutrients like magnesium and potassium that work synergistically with calcium.

 

Tips for success

  • Track symptoms: Keep a food diary to identify what works for you and help pinpoint your triggers. This will also help with reintroduction of dairy foods to see which ones (if any) you can tolerate and the portion sizes that work for you.
  • Read labels carefully: Many packaged foods contain hidden lactose.
  • Choose lactose-free versions of dairy products first, over plant alternatives, as these can still provide all the highly bioavailable nutrients of dairy with less processing and additives.

A lower lactose day on a plate

Here’s an example of how you might structure your day with lactose-free foods that are also rich in calcium:

Breakfast

  • Lactose-free milk porridge with chia seeds and almonds

Lunch

  • Salad with kale, avocado, chickpeas, tofu and tahini dressing, served with a calcium-fortified beverage

Snack

  • Lactose-free yoghurt with a handful of almonds

Dinner

  • Grilled salmon with stir-fried broccoli, carrots and capsicum on whole grain rice

Dessert

  • Calcium-fortified plant or lactose-free hot chocolate

FAQs

Will I have to avoid dairy for life if I’m lactose intolerant?

Not necessarily. Some people experience temporary lactose intolerance, especially after illnesses like gastroenteritis and may be able to reintroduce dairy into their diet over time. For those with permanent lactose intolerance, experimenting with what foods and how much you can tolerate is key. You can try small amounts of dairy to see if your tolerance improves, but for some, it may always be necessary to avoid larger servings of dairy.

Is lactose intolerance hereditary?

Yes, lactose intolerance is often genetic. In some populations, lactase production decreases naturally with age, leading to intolerance. If you have a family history of lactose intolerance, you may be more likely to experience it as well, though environmental factors and diet can also influence your body’s ability to digest lactose.

Can probiotics help with lactose intolerance?

Yes, probiotics may aid digestion and may help reduce symptoms of lactose intolerance. Certain probiotic strains, such as Lactobacillus acidophilus and Bifidobacterium, can support the breakdown of lactose in the digestive system. Including probiotic-rich foods like kefir, non-dairy yoghurts and sauerkraut may improve digestion and comfort for those with lactose intolerance.

Are there some dairy products I am able to eat if I’m lactose intolerant?

People with lactose intolerance can usually tolerate small amounts of dairy, such as hard cheeses (e.g. cheddar, parmesan) and yoghurts with live cultures, like acidophilus, which aid in digestion. The amount of lactose you can tolerate varies, so it’s best to experiment and keep track of your symptoms. Some people can also drink 100-200ml of milk without issues.

Are coconut and other dairy-free yoghurts healthy?

Dairy-free yoghurts made from coconut, almonds, or oats may not be as nutritionally complete as dairy yoghurt. Many coconut and nut-based yoghurts are low in protein and calcium and may be high in fats, especially coconut-based varieties. Soy-based yoghurts are the closest in nutrition to dairy, offering similar protein, carbs and calcium along with probiotics. Always check labels for calcium fortification.

The bottom line

Lactose intolerance is a common condition that can be managed through dietary adjustments. By experimenting with dairy product tolerance, trying lactose-free alternatives and ensuring sufficient calcium intake, people with lactose intolerance can live comfortably and maintain a nutritious well-rounded diet. Whether through small amounts of dairy, lactase enzyme supplements or plant-based substitutes, managing lactose intolerance doesn’t mean sacrificing taste or nutrition.
